title: One Dutch company sent nearly a million Europeans to Asia on 4,785 ships

cover.alt: A full-size replica of the 17th-century VOC ship Batavia, with tall masts and an ornate carved stern, moored at Lelystad.

body: The **Dutch East India Company**, the VOC, was chartered on 20 March 1602 with a 21-year monopoly on Dutch trade with Asia. It was one of the first joint-stock companies: any citizen of the Dutch Republic could buy in, 1,143 subscribers put up about 6.4 million guilders, and the trading of their shares grew into the Amsterdam Stock Exchange. The state let the company wage war, negotiate treaties, strike its own coins and found colonies. Between 1602 and 1796 it sent nearly a million Europeans to Asia on 4,785 ships and carried more than 2.5 million tonnes of Asian goods, dwarfing its English rival, which sailed 2,690 ships for about a fifth of the tonnage; it also took part in the slave trade. Smuggling, corruption and administrative costs finally bankrupted it, and when its charter expired on 31 December 1799 the state took over its possessions and its debts.

slides.alt: A wooden replica of the VOC ship Amsterdam floating in the Oosterdok harbour beside the National Maritime Museum in Amsterdam.
slides.caption: A replica of the Dutch East India Company (VOC) ship Amsterdam at the National Maritime Museum. The original sailed in the 18th century, late in the company's life.

slides.question: How many people subscribed to the VOC's founding capital in 1602?
slides.explanation: 1,143 subscribers, including 39 Germans and 301 people from the Southern Netherlands, with a minimum stake of 3,000 guilders. Together they raised about 6.4 million guilders.

slides.heading: Ships sent to Asia, 1602–1796
slides.note: The English company carried about one fifth of the VOC's tonnage

slides.heading: A company with the powers of a state

events.text: Charter expires; the state takes over

slides.question: What grew into the Amsterdam Stock Exchange?
slides.explanation: VOC shares could be bought by any citizen and were resold in open-air secondary markets. One of those markets became the Amsterdam Stock Exchange.
